t: Prime Number of Set Bits in Binary Representation
o: For each integer in [left, right], count its set bits (1s in binary) and check whether that count is prime. Since right <= 10^6 < 2^20, every number has at most 20 set bits, so the only possible prime counts are 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17, 19. In Example 1 (6..10), the counts are 2,3,1,2,2 — four are prime. In Example 2 (10..15), counts are 2,3,2,3,3,4 — five are prime. The small range of bit counts means primality can be checked with a tiny hardcoded set or sieve over 0..20.
k: right <= 10^6 implies at most 20 bits, so only primes up to 19 matter: {2,3,5,7,11,13,17,19}.
Popcount can be computed with built-ins (__builtin_popcount, Integer.bitCount) or via n & (n-1) trick in O(bits).
With at most ~10^4 numbers to check and O(20) work each, brute force is already optimal asymptotically.

a.i: Iterate every number in the range, count its set bits by repeatedly clearing the lowest set bit (n &= n-1), and test the count for primality by trial division up to sqrt(count). Counts are at most 20, so trial division is trivially fast.
s: For each x from left to right, compute c = popcount(x) using the n & (n-1) loop.
Check if c is prime via trial division from 2 to sqrt(c).
Increment the answer when c is prime; return it.
a.t: O((right - left + 1) * log(right)) — each popcount is O(log right) and primality is O(1) since counts <= 20.

a.i: Since counts never exceed 20, precompute which counts 0..20 are prime as a bitmask or boolean array once, then answer each query with an O(1) lookup after a built-in popcount. This removes repeated trial division and is the cleanest interview solution.
s: Build a boolean table isPrime[0..20] (or a bitmask like 665772 whose bits mark primes 2..19).
For each x in [left, right], compute c = popcount(x).
Add 1 to the answer iff isPrime[c]; return the total.
a.t: O((right - left + 1) * log(right)) — one popcount per number; lookups are O(1).
a.sp: O(1) — the prime set/table has constant size.

w: In an interview, lead with Approach 1 to show correctness, then mention that counts are bounded by 20 so primality becomes a constant-time lookup (Approach 2). Pitfalls: forgetting that 1 is not prime and 2 is prime; off-by-one on the inclusive range; assuming larger inputs need a sieve when the range length is at most 10^4 anyway. Edge cases: left == right, single-bit powers of two (count 1, not prime). Follow-ups might ask for huge ranges (use digit DP / combinatorial counting of numbers with k set bits) or computing popcount without built-ins.
